en: The Sūtra on King Bimbisāra’s Five Vows, translated by the layman Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi state during the Wu dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, together with five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a king of Rājagṛha named Bimbisāra. Having been the crown prince since his youth, he constantly harbored five wishes:
first, "May I become king while still young."
Second, "May there be a Buddha within my country";
third, "May I always go to and come from the presence of the Buddha";
fourth, "May I constantly hear the Buddha preach the sutras."
Fifth, "Upon hearing the sutra, his mind quickly attained understanding, and he realized the stage of Srotāpanna.
King Piṅgala attained all five of these vows.
At that time, to the north of the kingdom of Rājagṛha, there was another country named Kāśī.

Its king was named Prasenajit, who was exceptionally noble and sublime. In a previous life, he had once encountered a Buddha, received the Buddha’s teachings and the Way, and studied the sixfold division of the Sūtras.

What are the six constituents? First, there is earth within the body; second, there is water within the body; third, there is fire within the body; fourth, there is wind within the body; fifth, there is space within the body; and sixth, there is mind within the body.
Within the body, there are generally these six parts.

King Piṅgala and King Puṣkarasārin had never met in person during their lifetimes, yet they loved and respected each other from afar as if they were brothers; they constantly exchanged letters and maintained an uninterrupted flow of mutual gifts.
King Piṅgala constantly thought to himself:
"May I obtain an exceptionally rare and wonderful object to bestow upon King Puṣkarasārin.
King Puṣkarasārin also constantly thought to himself:
"May I obtain an exceptionally rare and wonderful object to present as a gift to King Piṅgiya.
Then, within the kingdom of King Puṣkarasārin, a lotus suddenly sprang forth; it had a thousand petals and was entirely golden in color.
He dispatched a messenger to present it to King Piṅgala.
Upon seeing the flower, King Piṅgala was greatly delighted and said,
"King Puṣya has sent me a most marvelous and extraordinary gift."
King Piṅgala wrote a letter to King Puṣkarasārin, saying:
"In my kingdom there is an abundance of gold, silver, and precious jewels; yet I do not regard these as true treasures."
"Now, among those born in my kingdom, there is one person who is a flower among men; his name is Buddha. His body is the color of purple-polished gold and possesses the thirty-two marks.

When King Puṣya read this and heard the word "Buddha," he was filled with great joy and leaped for gladness, such that the hair on his body stood on end—because he had seen the Buddha in a previous life, his hair stood on end.
King Pukkasāti wrote a letter to King Pingpisha, saying:
"I wish to hear in full the instructions and admonitions practiced by the Divine Buddha, which I shall duly follow.
I pray that you will fully inform me of your intentions."
After several days had passed, King Puṣya thought to himself:
"The life of a human being is unpredictable; it lasts but a moment between breaths.
I cannot wait any longer for Piṅgala’s reply; it would be better for me to go myself to see the Buddha."
King Pukkasāti ruled over ninety-nine small kingdoms, and the kings of these small states came to pay their court.

King Pukkasāti commanded all the minor kings, as well as his ministers, officials, and soldiers, to prepare their carriages and set out for the kingdom of Rājagṛha to the place where the Buddha was staying.
On the road, he encountered a letter from King Piṅgala, which stated:
"The Buddha teaches people to leave their homes, abandon their wives and children, sever their desires, shave off their hair and beards, don the dharma robes, and become śramaṇas."
Why is this? Because people are deluded, they engage in what ought not to be done; thus they are deluded.
From delusion, volitional formations arise.
From volitional formations comes consciousness;
from consciousness comes name-and-form;
from name-and-form come the six sense bases.
What are the six sense bases?
First, the eye; second, the ear; third, the nose; fourth, the tongue; fifth, the body; and sixth, the mind.
These are the six.
These six things are all directed outward:
the eye is directed toward forms;
The ear inclines toward sounds;
the nose toward fragrances;
the mouth toward flavors.
The body inclines toward delicacy and softness;
the mind inclines toward desire.
These are the six inclinations.
From the six sense bases arises contact;
from contact arise feeling and pleasure;
from feeling and pleasure arises craving.
From craving comes feeling;
from feeling comes becoming;
from becoming comes birth.
From birth arise old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress due to not obtaining what one desires; thus does this great mass of suffering follow from habitual practice.
Whoever is joined with this diligent toil is called a "person."
The wise person removes their own ignorance;
when ignorance is exhausted, all evils are eliminated;
when evils are eliminated, then karma is exhausted.
With the exhaustion of volitional formations, consciousness is exhausted; with the exhaustion of consciousness, name-and-form is exhausted;
with the exhaustion of name-and-form, the six sense bases are exhausted.
With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases;
with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases;
with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases.
With the exhaustion of craving comes the exhaustion of clinging; with the exhaustion of clinging comes the exhaustion of existence;
with the exhaustion of existence comes the exhaustion of birth.
Birth ceases; old age and death cease.
When old age and death have ceased, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress—the entire mass of great suffering that arises through habitual conditioning—cease as well, and one is no longer born.
Through non-arising, one attains the unconditioned path of Nirvana.
After King Puṣya has finished reading the book, he reflects to himself.
Late at night, after everyone has settled down, the ministers, officials, and commoners have all retired to bed; it is silent and without a sound.
He rose stealthily and fled, entering among the burial mounds where he shaved his own head, donned the dharma robes, and became a śramaṇa.
Having no food or alms bowl, he took the skull of a person who had died long ago from among the tombs, scrubbed it clean, rinsed it, and used it as an alms bowl.
Carrying this skull-bowl as his alms vessel, he traveled on until he reached the kingdom of King Pingbisha in Rājagṛha.
He stayed outside the city and, raising his head to look at the sun, thought:
"It is too late today to reach the Buddha's dwelling; I shall go tomorrow."
King Pukkasāti approached the potter and said,
"I wish to stay one night.
The potter replied:
"Excellent! My residence is fortunately spacious; there is a place for you to stay.
King Pukkasāti took a small grass mat from outside and entered, where he spread out a seat in a secluded corner and sat upon it, contemplating the five internal aggregates.
With his divine eye, the Buddha saw from Mount Śyāmāka that King Bimbisāra was approaching; he had arrived at the kingdom of Rājagṛha and was staying outside the city with a potter.
The Buddha thought: "King Bimbisāra’s life will end tomorrow; I fear we shall not meet again after he has passed away."
The Buddha immediately flew through the air and arrived at the gate of the potter’s house.
He addressed the potter, saying,
“I wish to stay for one night.”
The potter replied, “My house is fortunately large enough to accommodate you.
However, a certain śramaṇa has recently come to stay as a guest; if he agrees upon consultation with me, you may then remain and lodge here.”
The Buddha then went before King Pukkasāti and said:
"I requested lodging for one night from my host, who told me that he would inform you.
Would you be willing to allow me to stay for one night?"
Pukkasāti said, "I have only this small grass mat, which is just enough for me to sit upon.
This dwelling is fortunately spacious; you may stay here as you please."
The Buddha then personally gathered some small grass mats from his left and right and sat down in one place.
The Buddha sat upright for three nights, and Puṣya also sat upright.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"This Puṣkarasārin sits in profound stillness and silence; he is unmoving and unshakable.
The Buddha wished to test him and intended to go forward and ask: "For what reason have you become a śramaṇa?"
"What sutras and precepts have you received?
Which sutras do you delight in?
The Buddha rose and approached Puṣya, asking him this.
"Whose teaching did your master receive?
For what purpose do you act as śramaṇas?
Vakkula replied:
"I have heard that there is a Buddha whose clan name is Gautama; his father’s personal name is Śuddhodana, the King of Pure Radiance.
His son shaved off his hair and beard to become a śramaṇa and attained the Way of the Buddha."
I served him as my teacher.
It was for the sake of the Buddha that I became a śramaṇa.
The sūtras spoken by the Buddha have entered my heart, and I rejoice in them greatly.
The Buddha asked,
"Have you ever seen a Buddha before? Puṣya said:
“I have never seen him.
“Even if you had seen him, would you have been able to recognize him as the Buddha? Puṣya said:
"Even upon seeing him, one cannot recognize him.
The Buddha thought:
"This worthy man has become a śramaṇa for my sake."
"I shall further explain for you the *Sūtra on What is Known of Past Lives*, and then you will understand quickly.
The Buddha said to Puṣkarasārin:
"I shall preach the sūtra to you; its beginning is excellent, its middle is excellent, and its end is excellent."
"I shall explain for you the matter of the six constituent parts within the body;
listen well! Vakkali said, "Excellent!"
The Buddha said:
"The combination of these six factors constitutes the formation of a human body.
A human body consists of these six factors and possesses the capacity for perception and cognition."
There are eighteen matters by which human will is moved;
among these, there are four matters that practitioners of the Way ought to practice.
Once these have been practiced, the will no longer wavers.
When one’s resolve no longer wavers, one attains the Way;

having attained the Way, one is no longer born, no longer ages, no longer falls ill, and no longer dies in this present life, nor does one die again in future lives; furthermore, one no longer grieves, no longer worries, no longer becomes angry, no longer thinks, and no longer craves.
This is the way to transcend the world.
"Please explain how these six matters combined are designated as 'human.
Listen attentively!"
First is earth, second is water, third is fire, fourth is wind, fifth is space, and sixth is mind.
What is the element of earth?
The element of earth is of two kinds:
the internal earth-element and the external earth-element.
What is the earth element of the body?
It refers to the hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, spleen, kidneys, liver, lungs, intestines, and stomach;
all that is solid within the body constitutes the earth element.

The internal earth element and the external earth element together constitute the single element of earth; yet this internal and external earth is not the "earth" of a self. One who knows this should have no further craving or attachment.
You should contemplate this thoroughly, for by doing so, you will attain liberation through your own understanding.
"What is water? Water is of two kinds:
internal water and external water."
What constitutes the water element of the body?
It refers to tears, nasal mucus, saliva, pus, blood, sweat, fat, marrow, brain, and urine;
all the moist components within the body are the water element.
The water of the body and external water combine to become one water; the water of the body and external water are not "my" water. One who knows this should have no further craving or attachment.
You should contemplate this thoroughly to achieve self-liberation.
"What is fire? Fire is of two kinds:
bodily fire and external fire."
What is the fire of the body?
It refers to the warmth within the body and that which governs digestion in the abdomen;
all such heat within the body constitutes fire.
The fire of the body and external fire combine to become fire; yet the fire of the body and external fire are not "my" fire. One who knows this has nothing further to crave or love.
You should contemplate this deeply to achieve liberation for yourself.
"What is wind? Wind is of two kinds:
bodily wind and external wind."
What is the bodily wind?
It refers to the upward-moving wind, the downward-moving wind, the wind between the bones, the wind within the abdomen, the wind in the four limbs, and the wind of respiration;
all that arises within the body is wind.
The bodily winds and external winds combine to form wind; these bodily and external winds are not my winds. One who knows this has nothing further to crave or love.
You should contemplate this thoroughly to achieve liberation for yourself.
"What is emptiness? There are two categories of emptiness:
the emptiness of the body and the emptiness of the external."
What is meant by the emptiness of the body?

It refers to the emptiness of the eyes, the emptiness of the ears, the emptiness of the nose, the emptiness of the mouth, the emptiness of the throat, the emptiness of the abdomen, the emptiness of the stomach, and the emptiness of that through which food enters and exits.
This is the emptiness of the body.

The emptiness of the body and the emptiness of the external merge together as emptiness; the emptiness of the body and the emptiness of the external are the emptiness of non-self. Thus, there is nothing further for one who knows to crave or cling to.
One should contemplate this deeply to achieve self-liberation.
"The wise person who trains in the Path is able to discern the five constituents within the body; the remaining constituent is the mind.
When the mind is pure and free from desire, one reflects to oneself:"
"I am pure in this way.

If one aspires to ascend to the twenty-fifth heaven, the Ākāśānantyāyatana (Heaven of Infinite Space), one fears that even with a lifespan of thousands of kalpas in the twenty-fifth heaven, one will not attain liberation.

If one further aspires to ascend to the twenty-sixth heaven, the Vijñānānantyāyatana (Heaven of Infinite Consciousness), the lifespan there is again doubled compared to the twenty-fifth heaven; yet one fears that one will still not attain liberation.

If one further aspires to ascend to the twenty-seventh heaven, the Heaven of Non-conceptual Wisdom (*asaṃjñisattva*), where the lifespan is twice that of the twenty-sixth heaven, one fears still not attaining liberation;
if one further aspires to ascend to the twenty-eighth heaven, the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñika*), with a lifespan of eighty-four million *kalpas*, one fears still not attaining liberation.
His resolve was then weary of suffering; having lived for a long time without attaining liberation, he took up the path to *nirvāṇa*.
"What are the six things that are joined together? They are:
the eye joined with form, the ear with sound, the nose with fragrance, the tongue with flavor, the body with the smooth and soft, and the mind with cognition."
These are the six spheres.
What are the eighteen transformations of the mental faculty? They are:
the eye transforming upon beautiful forms, transforming upon ugly forms, and transforming upon neutral forms; [and so on for the other five faculties].
The ear is turned by pleasant sounds, turned by sorrowful sounds, and turned by unpleasant sounds;
the nose is turned by pleasant fragrances, turned by unpleasant fragrances, and turned by foul odors;
the tongue is turned by delicious flavors, turned by unpalatable flavors, and turned by flavorless things.
The body turns according to what is delicate or coarse, what is hard or soft, and what is cold or warm;
the mind turns according to wholesome matters, unwholesome matters, and worldly affairs.
This constitutes the eighteen transformations of aspiration.
What are the four matters that firmly restrain a person?
First is utmost sincerity; second is equanimity of mind; third is wisdom; and fourth is the eradication of all evils.
These are the four firm resolves.
That which the eyes crave and love brings happiness when obtained;
yet when that happiness departs from one, one realizes it has passed away.
From suffering one reaches suffering; one must know this as suffering.
When suffering has departed, one knows for oneself that one is liberated from suffering.
A person who practices suffering finds it difficult to attain happiness; therefore, one should contemplate the severing of all evil deeds.
Because one attains neither-pain-nor-pleasure, one knows for oneself that one is far removed from all suffering.
It is like two pieces of wood being rubbed together to produce fire; once the two pieces of wood are separated and each is placed aside, the fire is extinguished and the wood becomes cool.
When one is joined with affection and love, suffering arises; by casting off affection and love, one knows for oneself that one is liberated.

It is like a goldsmith who, having obtained fine gold, can at will fashion whatever exquisite objects he desires—whether bracelets, earrings, anklets, flower-bedecked ornaments, or a hundred other kinds—he is able to create them all.

A practitioner of the Way who maintains the mind should be like a goldsmith who can produce whatever he desires at will, without needing to rely on the desire to be born in the twenty-fifth, twenty-sixth, twenty-seventh, or twenty-eighth heaven.
Yet, upon careful examination, all things truly possess this nature: though they endure for a long time, they must inevitably perish; all shall pass away, for nothing is permanent.

Knowing that they will again pass away, one’s mind no longer turns toward them, no longer recollects them, no longer contemplates them, and no longer craves them—this is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The wise person reflects for themselves that it is precisely by this means that one becomes exalted;
when a person distances themselves from all evils, they are truly wise.
All things seen by the eye must pass away; there is nothing permanent. That which is unconditioned neither departs nor arrives again.
When a practitioner of the Way knows this, they place their faith in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as the ultimate sincerity.
Before attaining the Way, that which the body and mind produce—namely, what is cherished, loved, and delighted in—is abandoned once the Way is attained.
When a person discards all objects of affection and attachment, this is called the unconditioned.
"Because their will is set upon lust, they cannot escape;
because their will is set upon anger, they cannot escape;
because their will is set upon delusion, they cannot escape."

The practitioner who understands this abandons the mind of lust, abandons the mind of anger, and abandons the mind of delusion; they uproot the source of affection and craving, sever its branches, and cut off its stems so that it no longer grows or flourishes.
This is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

"Reflecting on oneself as having a self, the will moves again; reflecting on being without a self, the will moves again; reflecting on myself as handsome, the will moves again; reflecting on myself as not handsome, the will moves again."
A person anticipates for themselves: "Such is illness; such is suffering; such is pain; such is lack of liberation.
For this reason, one does not wish to dwell on many thoughts.
"This is what is called the essence of all suffering.
Vakkali did not originally know that this was the Buddha; it was only upon attaining the third stage of *anāgāmin* that he was able to recognize him as the Buddha.
He immediately rose and placed his head at the Buddha's feet, saying, "I was truly foolish and lacking in propriety; I have failed in my reverence.
The Buddha then manifested his own radiance and majestic spiritual power.
Pukkasāti then repented his own faults, saying,
"I am a foolish man.
The Buddha said:
"If you can repent of your transgressions and do good, I shall cause your faults to be removed.
Puṣkarasārin said,
"I pray that you accept me as a śramaṇa."
The Buddha asked,
"If you become a śramaṇa, will your robes and bowl be complete?
Puṣkarasārin replied:
"Not complete," the Buddha said.
"One whose robes and bowl are not complete cannot be a śramaṇa."
Vṛkasas said: "Yes.
Please go and prepare it."
The Buddha said,
"Excellent! Vakkali rose, paid homage to the Buddha, and circumambulated him three times.
The next day, Vakkali entered the city.
Not long after he had entered, a young cow with small teeth ran toward him and gored him with her horns.
The bhikṣus heard of this from one another and reported it to the Buddha, saying:
"Did the Buddha not preach the sūtras for the potter yesterday?
That śramaṇa, having prepared his robes and bowl before departing, was gored to death by a runaway ox; where will he go after death?"
The Buddha said:

“This great elder, when I preached the sutra for him, received and practiced it with his whole heart, and immediately attained the third path—Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, and Anāgāmin—and cast off the five hindrances:
first, lust; second, anger; third, sloth and torpor; fourth, restlessness and regret; and fifth, doubt and improper states of mind.”
In this life, he was reborn among the Ānāgāmins in the six heavens of the desire realm; there, he himself attained arhatship and passed away from the world.
Now, let all the bhikṣus together take the body of Puṣkarasārin, enshrine it well for burial, and erect a stūpa over it.
The bhikṣus then collectively accepted the Buddha’s instruction and immediately erected a stūpa for him.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sūtra, all the bhikṣus joined their palms and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Sūtra on King Bimbisāra’s Five Vows Spoken by the Buddha
